cards.front: Why is concurrency described as "arguably deterministic but effectively nondeterministic"?
cards.back: Correct code is possible in principle, but failures depend on timing and may never reproduce
cards.extra: The book's warning is that a program can pass every test and still be broken. Absence of a failure is not evidence of correctness here.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws InterruptedException {
int[] n = {0}; Runnable task = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) n[0]++; };
Thread a = new Thread(task), b = new Thread(task);
a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join();
} }

cards.back: Nothing about when the thread resumes after the delay — only that it does not run for at least that long
cards.extra: The OS scheduler decides when to wake it, and the thread may wait much longer. Sleep is for pacing, never for coordination.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws InterruptedException {
long before = System.nanoTime();
Thread.sleep(100);
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - before;
} }

cards.front: Why is synchronized needed on a shared counter?
cards.back: i++ is three steps (read, add, write), so two threads can interleave and lose an update
cards.extra: The lock makes the three steps atomic with respect to other synchronized code. Without it the final value is silently less than expected.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
class Ex {
  int count;
  synchronized void inc() { count++; }
}

cards.front: What does a Lock object give you that synchronized does not?
cards.back: Try-lock, timed lock, interruptible lock, and the ability to lock across methods
cards.extra: synchronized releases only when the block exits; a Lock is explicit, so you must release it in a finally block or you deadlock yourself.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
class Ex {
  final java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock lock = new java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock();
  boolean a() { return lock.tryLock(); }
  boolean b() throws InterruptedException { return lock.tryLock(1, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS); }
  void c() throws InterruptedException { lock.lockInterruptibly(); }
}

cards.front: What is the difference between notify() and notifyAll()?
cards.back: notify wakes one waiting thread; notifyAll wakes all of them to re-check their condition
cards.extra: Waking the wrong thread with notify leaves a valid waiter asleep forever. The safe default is notifyAll plus a while loop around wait().
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
class Ex {
  synchronized void signalAll() { notifyAll(); }
  synchronized void signalOne() { notify(); }
}

cards.front: Why must wait() be called inside a while loop?
cards.back: Because the thread can wake up without the condition being true — spurious wakeups and competing threads
cards.extra: Always re-test the condition after waking. An if around wait() is the classic concurrency bug in this chapter.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
class Ex {
  boolean ready;
  synchronized void await() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!ready) wait();
  }
}

cards.back: Producer/consumer handoff: put blocks when full, take blocks when empty
cards.extra: It removes the need to write wait/notify by hand. The queue becomes the only shared state, and its own locking is already correct.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue q = new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
q.put("item");
String item = q.take();
} }

cards.back: Blocks threads until a counter reaches zero, then releases them all at once
cards.extra: One-shot: it counts down, never up. Use it to wait for N tasks to finish before continuing, or to start N threads simultaneously.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch latch = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(2);
latch.countDown(); latch.countDown();
latch.await();
} }

cards.back: It is reusable — threads meet, then the barrier resets for the next round
cards.extra: Latch is one-shot and counts completions; barrier is a rendezvous point that can be crossed repeatedly, which suits iterative parallel algorithms.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier b = new java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier(2);
b.await();
b.await();
} }

cards.front: What does an ExecutorService change about starting threads?
cards.back: You submit tasks instead of managing threads; a pool reuses them
cards.extra: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) decouples task count from thread count, which is what makes a server survive many requests.

cards.front: What is a deadlock, in this book's terms?
cards.back: Two threads each holding a lock the other needs, waiting forever
cards.extra: It happens with two locks acquired in opposite orders. The fix is a global lock ordering, or a single lock guarding both resources.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
Object a = new Object(), b = new Object();
new Thread(() -> { synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) {} } }).start();
new Thread(() -> { synchronized (b) { synchronized (a) {} } }).start();
} }

cards.front: Why is volatile not enough for a counter?
cards.back: It guarantees visibility, not atomicity of read-modify-write
cards.extra: count++ on a volatile field still loses updates. Volatile suits a flag one thread writes and another reads; counting needs atomic or a lock.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  volatile int count;
  void inc() { count++; }
}
